# Omni Adapter

> The official adapter library for joining a ProtoPie **Connect Omni** stage from your own program — TypeScript/JavaScript (incl. React), Python, C#/.NET (incl. Unity), Kotlin/JVM/Android, Swift and Dart/Flutter — and exchanging real-time messages with prototypes, people and other programs over named channels. One credential (an adapter token, `cst_…`); values are primitives, objects travel as JSON strings. This file is written for AI coding assistants: read the first three sections, then only the section for your language — each language section stands on its own.

## Contents

2. [Rules that prevent most bugs](#rules-that-prevent-most-bugs)

[Concepts and the six-language name map](#concepts-and-the-six-language-name-map) — [name map](#name-map) · [lifecycle events per language](#lifecycle-events-per-language) · [sessions and names](#sessions-and-names) · [delivery](#delivery-acks-offline-queue-standby) · [latest and history](#latest-and-history)
4. Languages — [TypeScript / JavaScript](#typescript--javascript) (+ React) · [Python](#python) · [C# / .NET](#c--net) · [Kotlin / JVM / Android](#kotlin--jvm--android) · [Swift](#swift) · [Dart / Flutter](#dart--flutter)
5. [Errors and troubleshooting](#errors-and-troubleshooting)
6. [Roster, diagnostics, testing, CLI](#roster-diagnostics-testing-cli)
7. [Optional](#optional) — screens (Web View, screen broadcast, remote input), Unity checklist, Android Automotive input injection, links

## The credential

- **One value: an adapter token, `cst_…`.** An Editor or Owner of the stage creates it in the Connect web app: open the stage → **Share → Adapter keys → Create key**, then **Copy**. Copy appears only right after Create key and the token is shown once — if it is lost, create a new key. The token carries the server address and the stage id; its secret is an individually revocable adapter key (`ck_…`).
- The only other accepted form is that bare `ck_…` key plus explicit `url` and `stageId`. Anything else (a share link, a share token) is rejected with `ConfigError` before any network call.
- Read it from an environment variable or secret store — never hard-code or log it. Pass it exactly: whitespace around it (typically the newline a token file ends with) is rejected with `ConfigError: credential has leading or trailing whitespace`; an unset variable gives a `ConfigError` whose hint says so.
- The **key name** typed at Create key only labels the key in the key list. The name the stage shows is `displayName` in your code.
- Use one token per program and machine (revoking a token disconnects every program using it) — except a deliberate standby copy, which shares its active program's token (see [sessions and names](#sessions-and-names)).

## Rules that prevent most bugs

1. **Lifecycle events have different names in each language** — use the [table](#lifecycle-events-per-language). Only TypeScript and Python use reserved names on `on()`; in C#, Kotlin, Swift and Dart, `client.on("error", …)` subscribes to a *channel* called `error` and never fires for adapter errors.
2. **Values are primitives** — string, number, boolean, null. Objects go through the JSON helpers (`sendJSON` / `send_json` / `SendJsonAsync` / `sendJson`) and the receiver uses the matching `onJSON` helper. A non-primitive value fails that call with `ValidationError` (Swift's `Primitive` enum rejects it at compile time) — the push function `throttle()` returns included. **Prototypes and the Console send every value as a string** (`"42"`, not `42`) or `null` when the message carries none — convert before comparing; programs receive whatever type another program sent. A message a prototype, a Figma or Unity layer or the Console sends arrives with **its name as the channel** (`on('door.open')` fires) on servers from 2026-10-19; older servers deliver those on the channel `STUDIO` with the name in `messageId`, so a name subscription never fires there — to support one, subscribe to `STUDIO` (with `strictRouting`, declare `receives: ['STUDIO']`) and read the name from `msg.messageId`.
3. **Subscribe to errors and to the session end** in every unattended program, and print the code with `hint ?? message`: several codes carry no hint (`AckTimeout`, `ValidationError`, `SessionEnded`, some `ConfigError`s), and for some (`AckTimeout`) the message is only the code itself — say which call failed. C#, Kotlin and Swift print nothing on their own.
4. **Close the client on exit — on Ctrl+C (SIGINT) and on SIGTERM** (docker stop, systemd, kill). `close()` ends the client at the call and leaves the stage — it waits up to 1 s for the server to confirm — so the seat and the name are freed at once. It **drops queued fire-and-forget sends**: to be sure the last values went out, await an acked send or wait until `queuedCount` is 0 first. A program that dies without `close()` leaves its seat for about 10 s (the server's guest grace — 8 s on servers before 2026-10-19); the same key keeps its name on restart (older servers renamed such a restart to `name (2)`).
5. **A live session must exist** when you connect, otherwise `connect` fails with `RoomEnded`: someone with edit rights opens the stage in Connect, or you connect with a key created with **Let adapters start a session** turned on (Share → Adapter keys).
6. **No self-echo.** The server never sends your own messages back to you, so your handlers never see them and UI lists need optimistic appends. `latest()` folds your own sends in locally — it is not proof that a send went out; use `ack: true` or watch from a second connection.
7. **History re-seeds state, it never re-fires triggers.** After a reconnect `latest()`/`history()` are re-seeded and the history event fires, but nothing missed is replayed into channel handlers. Read state channels with `latest()` when the state becomes `connected`; trigger channels are at-most-once across a disconnect.
8. **`connected` does not mean messages are flowing.** Check `state` and `queuedCount` together — see [connected but nothing happens](#connected-but-nothing-happens).
9. **Never block inside a callback.** Callbacks run one at a time in arrival order; a blocked callback holds back every later message and every ack reply. Each language section says which thread you are on and how to hop.
10. **Reuse one client, and stay under 60 messages a second.** Each connection takes one guest seat of the stage's cap; never connect per message. The server takes at most 60 messages a second per connection — coalesce high-rate sources with `throttle()`, and never use `ack: true` for a stream (acked sends go one per round trip).
11. **Declare every channel the program uses — always, not only for `strictRouting`.** Each channel it sends on goes in `sends`, each channel it subscribes to in `receives`; when you add a send or a handler later, add its channel to the declaration in the same change. Connect learns a program's channels from this declaration before any message flows: the Backstage node's port chips (flow pulses light up only for declared channels) and `listeners()` read it, and a Web View page's declaration is what turns its channels on in the layer's Stage messages rules. An undeclared channel still flows, so a missing entry does not fail where you can see it — it shows up later as a connection Backstage does not draw and `listeners()` does not report. Up to 32 names each; omit a field only when the program never sends (or never receives) anything — an empty list is a `ConfigError`. Use exact names; a wildcard (`robot.*`) is allowed in `receives` only without `strictRouting` and outside a Web View page, for names you cannot know in advance. If a list would pass 32, tell the user instead of declaring part of it. `strictRouting: true` needs a non-empty `receives` of exact names; the server then delivers only those (plus messages targeted at you), and subscribing to anything else receives nothing.
12. **When connecting fails, run the doctor before changing code** — it names the broken step. It checks the connection, not delivery: a green doctor plus a silent peer means the channel name, the routing or the receiving side is wrong.
13. **An `AckTimeout` does not prove the server missed the message** — nor does `QueueOverflow`, `Standby` or `SessionEnded` on a queued acked send that had already gone out once; a blind retry can publish it twice.

## Concepts and the six-language name map

A **stage** is a shared Connect workspace; prototypes, people and programs on it exchange messages on dot-separated **channels** (`door.open`, `line3.temp`) — what ProtoPie calls a *message*. A **session** is a stage that is running now. Every connected program appears as a node on the stage's **Backstage** canvas and as the *Source* of its messages in the **Console**. In subscriptions `*` matches one or more dot segments: `robot.*` matches `robot.arm` and `robot.arm.pos`; `*` alone matches everything.

### Name map

| Concept | TypeScript | Python | C# | Kotlin | Swift | Dart |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| connect | `await connect({…})` | `await omni_adapter.connect(…)` | `await Connect.ToStageAsync(new ConnectOptions {…})` | `connect(ConnectOptions(…))` (suspend) | `try await connect(ConnectOptions(…))` | `await connect(ConnectOptions(…))` |
| send a primitive | `send(ch, v, { ack: true })` | `await send(ch, v, ack=True)` | `await SendAsync(ch, v, ack: true)` | `send(ch, v, ack = true)` | `try await send(ch, .double(x), ack: true)` | `await send(ch, v, ack: true)` |
| send an object | `sendJSON` | `send_json` | `SendJsonAsync` | `sendJson` (Map/List/`JSONObject`/`JSONArray`) | `sendJSON` (`[String: Any]`, `[Any]`) | `sendJson` |
| subscribe | `on(p, cb)` → unsubscribe fn | `on(p, cb)` → unsubscribe fn, or `@client.on(p)` | `On(p, cb)` → `IDisposable` | `on(p) { }` → `Closeable` | `await on(p) { }` → `Subscription` | `on(p, cb)` → unsubscribe fn |
| receive JSON | `onJSON(p, (value, msg) => …)` | `on_json(p, cb(value, msg))` | `OnJson<T>(p, (value, msg) => …)` | `onJson(p) { value, msg -> }` | `onJSON(p) { value, msg in }` | `onJson(p, (value) {…})` |
| lifecycle events | `on('error', …)` | `on("error", …)` | `client.Error += …` | `events` flow, `state` flow | `events()` stream | `onEvent('error', …)` |
| last value | `latest(ch)` → `undefined` if unknown | `latest(ch)` → `None` | `Latest(ch)` → `object?` | `latest(ch)` → `Any?` | `await latest(ch)` → `Primitive?` | `latest(ch)` → `Object?` |
| state now | `state` (string) | `state` (str) | `State` (string) | `state.value` (String) | `await state` (`TransportState`) | `state` (`TransportState`) |
| backlog · standby | `queuedCount` · `standby` | `queued_count` · `standby` | `QueuedCount` · `Standby` | `queuedCount` · `standby` | `await queuedCount` · `await standby` | `queuedCount` · `standby` |
| close | `await close()` | `await close()` | `await CloseAsync()` / `Dispose()` | `close()` (suspend) | `await close()` | `await close()` |
| doctor | `runDoctor` + `formatDoctorReport` | `run_doctor` + `format_doctor_report` | `Doctor.RunAsync` + `Doctor.FormatReport` | `runDoctor` + `formatDoctorReport` | `runDoctor(credential:)` + `formatDoctorReport` | `runDoctor` + `formatDoctorReport` |
| ack timeout (default 15 s; finite, > 0, ≤ 2^31−1 ms — else `ConfigError`) | `ackTimeoutMs` | `ack_timeout_s` | `AckTimeout` (`TimeSpan`) | `ackTimeoutMs` | `ackTimeout` (seconds) | `ackTimeout` (`Duration`) |

Also in every language (snake_case in Python; PascalCase plus `Async` on awaitables in C#): `history(pattern?)`, `historyJSON(ch)`, `latestJSON(ch)`, `members()`, `listeners(ch)`, `sendTo(participantId, ch, v)`, `throttle(ch, hz)` (Swift and Dart: `hz:`), `me`, `diagnostics()`, `note(code, message, level)`, `ping()`. The JSON receive helpers silently skip values that are not valid JSON strings.

### Lifecycle events per language

| Event | TypeScript / Python | C# (.NET event) | Kotlin (`client.events`) | Swift (`client.events()`) | Dart (`onEvent`) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| state changed | `'stateChange'` → state string | `StateChanged` (`string`) | `ClientEvent.StateChange(state)`, or collect `client.state` | `.stateChange(TransportState)` | `'stateChange'` → `String` |
| error | `'error'` → `AdapterError` | `Error` (`AdapterError`) | `ClientEvent.Failure(error)` | `.failure(AdapterError)` | `'error'` → `AdapterError` |
| someone joined | `'memberJoin'` → `Member` | `MemberJoined` (`Member`) | `ClientEvent.MemberJoin(member)` | `.memberJoin(Member)` | `'memberJoin'` → `Member` |
| someone left | `'memberLeave'` → participant id | `MemberLeft` (`string`) | `ClientEvent.MemberLeave(participantId)` | `.memberLeave(String)` | `'memberLeave'` → `String` |
| history re-seeded | `'history'` → messages | `HistoryReplaced` (`IReadOnlyList<StageMessage>`) | `ClientEvent.HistoryReplaced(history)` | `.historyReplaced([StageMessage])` | `'history'` → `List<StageMessage>` |
| session over | `'ended'` → reason or none | `Ended` (`string?`) | `ClientEvent.Ended(reason)` | `.ended(String?)` | `'ended'` → `String?` |
| offline queue dropped its oldest | `'queueOverflow'` → `PublishInput` | `QueueOverflow` | `ClientEvent.QueueOverflow(input)` | `.queueOverflow(PublishInput)` | `'queueOverflow'` |

- Python uses the **same camelCase strings** as TypeScript (`"stateChange"`, not `"state_change"` — that would be a channel).
- Kotlin `events` is a hot `SharedFlow` with no replay and a 256-event buffer that drops the oldest. Nothing can subscribe before `connect()` returns, so the `connected` transition is already gone: launch collectors with `start = CoroutineStart.UNDISPATCHED` right after `connect()` (subscribed before the next line runs) and read `client.state.value` / `history()` for what came before. One `launch` per collector — `collect` never returns. Swift: each `events()` stream sees only events after the call, buffers the newest 256 and finishes right after `.ended`. Dart: an unknown `onEvent` name silently never fires.
- `ended` reasons (same strings everywhere): `client-closed` (you closed it); `rejoin-abandoned: <code>` (waiting cannot fix it — `AuthRevoked` when the key was revoked or expired, `ProtocolVersionMismatch`, `ClientAheadOfServer`, `ConfigError`, `ValidationError`); with `autoRejoin` off also the server's own reason, `room-ended`, `server-disconnect` (the server cut the connection) or `reauth-failed`. `ended` is final — build a new client to connect again.
- There is no standby-change event: read `standby`, or watch for the `standby` / `active` codes in `diagnostics()` or the `onLog` sink.

### Sessions and names

- **Who starts a session.** An Editor or Owner opening the stage in Connect starts it; people who join through a share link cannot. The person who created the stage holds the session: when they close the stage, it ends about a minute later — even with programs connected. A key created with **Let adapters start a session** turned on (Share → Adapter keys — a key keeps the setting it was issued with) can start the session itself, and while such a key exists the creator is just another participant: the session stays open while anyone — person or program, the creator included — is connected and closes a few minutes (5 by default) after the last one leaves. Revoking the last such key — or its expiry, noticed within 15 s — while no Editor or Owner is connected ends the session about a minute later. Without such a key the session ends about a minute after its creator leaves (Editors still inside do not hold it), and a session an Editor opened without the creator ends about a minute after the last Editor leaves — programs connected or not.
- **When a session ends under a connected client**, the client does not end: with `autoRejoin` (on by default) it reports `reconnecting`, queues sends and joins the next session. Pass `autoRejoin: false` for a one-shot script that should finish with the session. A revoked or expired key still ends it (`rejoin-abandoned: AuthRevoked`).
- **`displayName`** (1–64 characters, default `Omni adapter`) is how the stage shows your program and how screen layers find it. Keep it stable — the participant id changes on every run. The same adapter key is never renamed — a restart keeps its name. Another **program** connected under the same name with a **different** key makes yours join as `name (2)`; for an adapter that joins with `providesView: 'stream'`, so does a name whose Adapter Stream layer is bound to another adapter key that is still valid — usually a rotated key whose old copy was never revoked: revoke it. Print `me.displayName` after connecting to see the name you got. A person who takes a program's name is the one renamed. (Older servers, from before same-key name sharing, renamed a restart that came within a few seconds of an unclean exit to `name (2)`.)
- **One active instance per name (`exclusiveName: true`)**, for a failover pair. Both copies must use the **same adapter key**; the newest connection is active and the others are standby: standby keeps receiving, stops sending, and takes over when the active one leaves. A copy with a different key joins as `name (2)` and its `exclusiveName` is ignored. Leave it off for crowds that share a name on purpose.

### Delivery: acks, offline queue, standby

- **Fire-and-forget by default.** `ack: true` waits for the **server's** acknowledgement — not a peer's — and fails with `AckTimeout` after 15 s (configurable). A direct acked send still waiting when the connection closes or drops fails with `AckTimeout` at once (all six) and is not re-sent; a queued acked send stays in the queue and goes out again after the reconnect — so an `AckTimeout` never proves the server didn't get it. Queued acked sends fail with `SessionEnded` when the client ends. The same caution holds for a queued acked send that went out just before a drop and is later failed with `QueueOverflow`, `Standby` or `SessionEnded`: on a queued acked send, none of these codes proves the server missed it.
- **Fire-and-forget is at-most-once — direct or queued.** It asks for no ack, so the adapter never learns that the server refused it (rate limit included), and a send lost to a drop right after it went out is not retried: nothing is thrown or recorded. Only acked sends see the server's answer: the call fails with the code (a direct acked send also leaves `send-dropped` in `diagnostics()`).
- **60 messages a second per connection.** The server accepts at most 60 messages a second from one connection and silently drops fire-and-forget messages over that. The adapter mirrors the limit with a token bucket — 60 per second, bursts of up to 30 — on every send, direct or queued: with no token free, the send waits in the queue. A source that keeps sending faster than 60/s fills the queue; the oldest items are dropped (the queue-overflow event fires for each; `diagnostics()` notes `queue-overflow` once per episode, again only after the queue has drained to half its limit) and the newest value still gets through. The queue drains at 60 a second, so a full default queue (1000) takes about 17 s to empty — and after a disconnect a sender at 60/s or more stays that far behind (up to `queueLimit` ÷ 60 seconds): throttle the source or lower `queueLimit`. The burst of 30 absorbs about half a second of network clumping. Acked sends go one per round trip — never use `ack: true` for a high-rate stream.
- **While disconnected, reconnecting or backing off**, sends queue (1000 by default; overflow drops the oldest as above and fails a dropped acked send with `QueueOverflow`) and flush in order once sending can resume, as fast as the bucket allows: fire-and-forget items go out without waiting for acks, an acked item waits for its server answer before the next one goes. A fire-and-forget send returns as soon as it is queued — **except in TypeScript**, where an awaited send that got queued resolves only when it is flushed (or dropped); do not `await` sends in a TypeScript sampling loop.
- **`close()` drops queued fire-and-forget sends** (queued acked sends fail with `SessionEnded`). To be sure the last values went out, await an acked send or wait until `queuedCount` is 0 before closing. `replay()`/`simulate()` and the CLI's `replay`/`simulate` already wait for the queue to drain (giving up after 15 s without progress), and those CLI commands exit 1 if anything is still queued.
- **`TooManyRequests`**, seen only on acked sends (the bucket makes it rare; `ensureStreamLayer()` throws it on a 429 — that one is yours to retry): the adapter backs off (1 s, doubling, up to 60 s) and re-queues silently — no `send-dropped`. You recognise it as: connected, `queuedCount > 0`, no `send-dropped`, not standby.
- **Standby.** New sends while standby are dropped (fire-and-forget) or rejected with `Standby` (`ack: true`) — never deferred. When an instance **becomes** standby (after a reconnect or when presence changes), everything it had queued is dropped too: fire-and-forget discarded (the `standby` entry in `diagnostics()` ends with `— dropped N queued sends`), acked sends rejected with `Standby`. A later promotion therefore sends nothing stale. After each (re)connect with `exclusiveName`, the adapter needs one roster round trip to learn whether it is standby; sends made meanwhile are held (sharing `queueLimit`), then queued if this instance is active (or the judgment failed) or treated by the standby rule.
- **`throttle(channel, hz)`** returns a push function that coalesces to at most `hz` sends per second (the last value wins). It validates the channel and value at the call and throws `ValidationError` for a bad one (a push after `close()` does not throw); delivery after that is fire-and-forget. There is no JSON variant — push the JSON string yourself (`JSON.stringify(obj)`).
- **JSON helpers**: a value that cannot be encoded (a cycle, an unsupported type) fails the call with `ValidationError` (TypeScript: the returned promise rejects; elsewhere the call throws). `NaN`/`Infinity` are rejected the same way in five languages; TypeScript's `JSON.stringify` turns them into `null`.

### latest and history

- `history(pattern?)` is the server's replay ring (the last 1000 messages by default), re-seeded on every (re)join. It is not storage.
- `latest(channel)` is the last value of each of the **1000 most recently updated channels**: seeded from the history snapshot, updated by live messages, and by your own sends once they go out (an acked send once the server acks it, a queued send when it is flushed). It is empty for a channel never seen, one pushed out by newer channels, or one missing from the snapshot after a reconnect.
- **Callback order**: in all six languages callbacks run one at a time in arrival order. Swift skips the oldest message callbacks once 1000 are waiting (`latest()` stays exact; signaling and presence are never skipped). Python async callbacks start in arrival order but interleave after their first `await`.

## TypeScript / JavaScript

**Install** — from npm. ESM-only, Node 22+ or any bundler:

```bash
npm install @studioxid/omni-adapter   # package.json needs "type": "module"
npx tsx main.ts                      # or compile with tsc first
```


**A complete program** — connect, lifecycle, receive, send, exit cleanly:

```ts
import { connect, isAdapterError, runDoctor, formatDoctorReport, type ConnectClient } from '@studioxid/omni-adapter';

const token = process.env.CONNECT_TOKEN ?? '';

async function join(): Promise<ConnectClient> {
  try {
    return await connect({
      secretKey: token,
      displayName: 'line3-controller',          // what the stage shows; keep it stable
      receives: ['door.state', 'robot.status'], // every channel it subscribes to (rule 11)
      sends: ['door.open', 'robot.target'],     // every channel it sends on
    });
  } catch (err) {
    if (!isAdapterError(err)) throw err;
    console.error(`connect failed: ${err.code}: ${err.hint ?? err.message}`);
    console.error(formatDoctorReport(await runDoctor(token)));   // names the broken step
    process.exit(1);
  }
}

const client = await join();
console.log(`joined as ${client.me?.displayName}`);   // "line3-controller (2)" if the name was taken
let timer: ReturnType<typeof setInterval> | undefined;
const stop = async () => { clearInterval(timer); await client.close(); };   // then nothing holds Node open
process.once('SIGINT', () => void stop());    // Ctrl+C
process.once('SIGTERM', () => void stop());   // docker stop, systemd, kill

// Lifecycle events are reserved names on the same on() (TypeScript and Python only).
client.on('error', (err) => console.error(`adapter error ${err.code}: ${err.hint ?? err.message}`));
client.on('stateChange', (state) => console.log(`state: ${state}`));
client.on('ended', (reason) => {
  if (reason === 'client-closed') return;      // our own close()
  console.error(`session over: ${reason ?? 'ended'}`);
  process.exitCode = 1;
  void stop();
});

client.on('door.state', (msg) => console.log(`door.state = ${String(msg.value)}`));
client.onJSON('robot.status', (value) => {     // value is unknown — cast it, or use typed channels
  console.log((value as { pose: number[] }).pose);
});

try {
  await client.send('door.open', true, { ack: true });   // resolves when the server acks
} catch (err) {
  if (!isAdapterError(err)) throw err;
  const why = err.hint ?? err.message;   // AckTimeout carries neither a hint nor more than its code
  console.error(`door.open failed: ${why === err.code ? err.code : `${err.code}: ${why}`}`);
}
// Un-awaited sends are fire-and-forget; attach a catch so a rejection is not unhandled.
client.sendJSON('robot.target', { x: 0, y: 0 }).catch((err: unknown) => console.error(err));

const pushTarget = client.throttle('robot.target', 20);   // at most 20 sends/s, last value wins
timer = setInterval(() => pushTarget(JSON.stringify({ x: Math.random(), y: Math.random() })), 10);   // no throttleJSON
```

**Types.** `StageMessage` is `{ channel, value, sourceParticipantId, timestamp, messageId? }`; `timestamp` is the server's stamp in epoch milliseconds, comparable across machines. `latest(ch)` returns `string | number | boolean | null | undefined`; `latestJSON<T>(ch)` and `historyJSON<T>(ch)` take a type parameter (no runtime validation), `onJSON` does not — its value is `unknown`. Typed channels make the JSON helpers infer per channel: `connect<{ 'robot.status': Pose }>({ … })`. `members()` includes you. Unsubscribe functions are plain `() => void` (there is no `Unsubscribe` export). Other exports: `ConnectOptions`, `ConnectClient`, `Primitive`, `Member`, `Listeners`, `AdapterError`, `isAdapterError`, `LogEntry`, `LogLevel` (`'debug' | 'info' | 'warn' | 'error'`), `MemoryStage`, `replay`, `simulate`, `buildReport`, `measureLatency`, `startScreenBroadcast`.

**Pitfalls**

- **An open client keeps the Node process alive.** A long-running adapter needs nothing extra; a one-shot script must `await client.close()` or it never exits. After `await client.close()` (and with your own timers cleared) the process exits by itself; do not call `process.exit()` before `close()` has finished.
- `close()` returns a `Promise<void>` that never rejects. The client ends at the call — later sends reject with `SessionEnded`, queued acked sends reject with `SessionEnded` right then, `ended` fires — and the promise settles once the server confirms the leave (at most about 1 s). Attach handlers to acked sends **before** `await client.close()`, or their rejection is unhandled. React cleanup: `return () => { void client.close(); };` (`() => () => client.close()` no longer type-checks with `@types/react` 19).
- `send()`/`sendJSON()` return promises: await them or attach `.catch` — an un-awaited rejection is unhandled (Node's default ends the process). Validation errors (bad value, closed client) reject the returned promise.
- Callbacks run on the event loop in arrival order; a long synchronous handler delays everything, ack replies included.
- Options worth knowing: `exclusiveName`, `strictRouting`, `autoRejoin` (default `true`), `ackTimeoutMs`/`joinTimeoutMs` (15000), `transports: ['polling']` (proxies that block WebSocket), `onLog` (stream the diagnostics ring into your logger), `queueLimit`, `osHostname`.
- In a browser page the token is visible to every visitor. For a page embedded in a Connect Omni stage use a Web View layer, which needs no credential ([Optional](#web-view-and-the-engine-profile)); otherwise use a token you are ready to revoke.

**React** (`react` 18+ is an optional peer dependency). The provider connects on mount and closes on unmount; your own sends are not echoed into `useChannelJSON` — append them to local state.

```tsx
import { ConnectProvider, useConnect, useChannelJSON } from '@studioxid/omni-adapter/react';

function Chat() {
  const { client, state, error } = useConnect();   // client is null until joined
  const messages = useChannelJSON<{ text: string }>('chat.message');   // history backlog + live
  if (error) return <p>{error.hint ?? error.message}</p>;
  return (
    <div>
      <p>{state}</p>
      {messages.map((m, i) => <p key={i}>{m.text}</p>)}
      <button onClick={() => void client?.sendJSON('chat.message', { text: 'hi' })}>send</button>
    </div>
  );
}

export const App = ({ token }: { token: string }) => (
  <ConnectProvider secretKey={token} displayName="dashboard" receives={['chat.message']} sends={['chat.message']}>
    <Chat />
  </ConnectProvider>
);
```

Other hooks: `useMembers`, `useLatest`, `useLatestJSON`, `useHistoryJSON`, `useChannelEvent`, `useThrottledSend`, `useConnectClient`.

## Python

**Install** — Python 3.10+:

```bash
pip install omni-adapter
```

The module is `omni_adapter`; the same package installs the `omni-adapter` CLI (`python -m omni_adapter …` when the npm CLI of the same name is also on PATH).

**A complete program** — a sensor bridge that also obeys a command channel:

```python
import asyncio
import os
import random
import sys
import time
from typing import Optional

import omni_adapter


def read_sensor() -> float:  # stands in for a blocking hardware read
    time.sleep(0.05)
    return round(21.0 + random.uniform(-0.5, 0.5), 2)


async def main() -> int:
    token = os.environ.get("CONNECT_TOKEN", "")
    try:
        client = await omni_adapter.connect(
            secret_key=token, display_name="line3-sensor",
            receives=["hvac.setTemp"], sends=["sensor.temperature", "hvac.status"],
        )
    except omni_adapter.AdapterError as err:
        print(f"connect failed: {err.code}: {err.hint or err.message}", file=sys.stderr)
        print(omni_adapter.format_doctor_report(await omni_adapter.run_doctor(token)), file=sys.stderr)
        return 1
    print(f"joined as {client.me.display_name if client.me else '?'}")
    stop, exit_code = asyncio.Event(), 0

    # Lifecycle events: the SAME camelCase names as TypeScript, on the same on().
    client.on("error", lambda err: print(f"adapter error {err.code}: {err.hint or err.message}", file=sys.stderr))
    client.on("stateChange", lambda state: print(f"state: {state}"))

    @client.on("ended")
    def on_ended(reason: Optional[str]) -> None:
        nonlocal exit_code
        if reason != "client-closed":
            print(f"session over: {reason}", file=sys.stderr)
            exit_code = 1
            stop.set()

    @client.on("hvac.setTemp")  # async: may await client calls (a sync callback must not — see pitfalls)
    async def on_set_temp(msg: omni_adapter.StageMessage) -> None:
        print(f"hvac.setTemp = {msg.value!r}")
        await client.send_json("hvac.status", {"target": msg.value, "ok": True})

    push = client.throttle("sensor.temperature", 5)  # at most 5 sends/s, last value wins

    async def sensor_loop() -> None:
        while True:
            push(await asyncio.to_thread(read_sensor))  # blocking I/O off the event loop
            await asyncio.sleep(0.2)

    task = asyncio.create_task(sensor_loop())
    # Ctrl+C / SIGTERM → leave cleanly: the first signal sets `stop`, a second exits at once. Needed on
    # Python 3.10 (asyncio.run would cancel the socket before `finally` runs); works on Windows too.
    with omni_adapter.stop_on_signals(stop.set):
        try:
            await stop.wait()
        finally:
            task.cancel()
            await client.close()  # leave the stage, so a restart keeps the name
    return exit_code


if __name__ == "__main__":
    try:
        sys.exit(asyncio.run(main()))
    except KeyboardInterrupt:
        pass
```

**Types.** `StageMessage` has `channel`, `value`, `source_participant_id`, `timestamp`, `message_id`; `Member` has `participant_id`, `display_name`, … (snake_case). `latest(ch)` returns `None` when unknown. `on(name, cb)` returns an unsubscribe function; the decorator form returns your function (remove it with `client.off(name, fn)`). `on_json` callbacks get `(value, msg)`. Options are snake_case keywords: `exclusive_name`, `strict_routing`, `auto_rejoin`, `ack_timeout_s`, `join_timeout_s`, `transports=["polling"]`, `on_log`, `queue_limit`, `os_hostname`.

**Pitfalls**

- **asyncio, one thread.** Callbacks run on the event loop in arrival order. A sync callback must not block (`time.sleep`, a blocking serial read) — it stalls every later message and ack. Blocking I/O belongs in `await asyncio.to_thread(...)`.
- **A sync callback cannot await.** Calling `client.send(...)` there only creates a coroutine that never runs ("coroutine … was never awaited") — nothing is sent. Make the callback `async def` (the adapter runs it and keeps it alive), or `asyncio.create_task(...)` and keep a reference to the task.
- **From another thread** (a serial reader, a GUI): `asyncio.run_coroutine_threadsafe(client.send(ch, v), loop)`.
- `send`/`send_json` raise `ValidationError` for a bad value; `send_json` emits compact JSON and rejects `NaN`/`Infinity`.
- **Ctrl+C without `stop_on_signals`** on Python 3.10: `asyncio.run` cancels the adapter's own tasks first, so the leave from `close()` never reaches the server and the name frees itself only a few seconds later (Python 3.11+ delivers it either way). A SIGTERM (`docker stop`, systemd) without a handler ends the process at once on every version. `with omni_adapter.stop_on_signals(stop.set):` fixes both (SIGTERM exists on POSIX only — Windows has Ctrl+C) and restores the previous handlers when the block ends; a second signal exits at once. After the first signal, a send already waiting for its ack keeps going until it settles (at most the ack timeout).

## C# / .NET

**Install** — netstandard2.0 + net8.0:

```bash
dotnet add package StudioXid.OmniAdapter
```


Namespace `StudioXid.OmniAdapter`. Unity: see the [Unity checklist](#unity).

**A complete program** (`Program.cs`, a .NET 8 console app):

```csharp
using System.Runtime.InteropServices;
using StudioXid.OmniAdapter;

var token = Environment.GetEnvironmentVariable("CONNECT_TOKEN") ?? "";
ConnectClient client;
try
{
    client = await Connect.ToStageAsync(new ConnectOptions
    {
        SecretKey = token, DisplayName = "line3-panel",
        Receives = new[] { "ui.mode", "robot.status", "panel.ping" },
        Sends = new[] { "door.open", "panel.state" },
    });
}
catch (AdapterError err)
{
    Console.Error.WriteLine($"connect failed: {err.Code}: {err.Hint ?? err.Message}");
    Console.Error.WriteLine(Doctor.FormatReport(await Doctor.RunAsync(token)));
    return 1;
}
Console.WriteLine($"joined as {client.Me?.DisplayName}");
var stop = new TaskCompletionSource<string?>(TaskCreationOptions.RunContinuationsAsynchronously);   // null = we stop

// Ctrl+C and SIGTERM → leave cleanly.
Console.CancelKeyPress += (_, e) => { e.Cancel = true; stop.TrySetResult(null); };
using var sigterm = PosixSignalRegistration.Create(PosixSignal.SIGTERM, ctx => { ctx.Cancel = true; stop.TrySetResult(null); });

// Lifecycle: .NET events. client.On("error", …) would subscribe to a CHANNEL named "error".
client.Error += err => Console.Error.WriteLine($"adapter error {err.Code}: {err.Hint ?? err.Message}");
client.StateChanged += state => Console.WriteLine($"state: {state}");
client.Ended += reason => stop.TrySetResult(reason ?? "ended");

// Server events arrive on the socket receive thread, one at a time — never block here.
client.On("ui.mode", msg => Console.WriteLine($"ui.mode = {msg.Value}"));
client.OnJson<RobotStatus>("robot.status", (status, msg) => Console.WriteLine($"pose {string.Join(",", status.pose)}"));
// An async handler is async void: catch inside it, or an escaping exception kills the process.
client.On("panel.ping", async msg =>
{
    try { await client.SendAsync("panel.state", "pong", ack: true); }
    catch (AdapterError e)
    {
        var why = e.Hint ?? e.Message;   // AckTimeout carries neither a hint nor more than its code
        Console.Error.WriteLine("panel.state failed: " + (why == e.Code ? e.Code : e.Code + ": " + why));
    }
});

try
{
    await client.SendAsync("door.open", true, ack: true);
    await client.SendJsonAsync("panel.state", new { mode = "ready", screen = 1 });
}
catch (AdapterError err)
{
    var why = err.Hint ?? err.Message;
    Console.Error.WriteLine("send failed: " + (why == err.Code ? err.Code : err.Code + ": " + why));
}

var ended = await stop.Task;
await client.CloseAsync();   // leaves the stage (≤ 1 s); Dispose() does the same without waiting
if (ended is null or "client-closed") return 0;
Console.Error.WriteLine($"session over: {ended}");
return 1;

record RobotStatus(double[] pose);   // property names go on the wire as written (case-sensitive)
```

**Types.** `StageMessage` has `Channel`, `Value`, `SourceParticipantId`, `Timestamp`, `MessageId`. `Value` and `Latest(ch)` are `object?` holding a `string`, `double`, `long`, `bool` or `null`. `On` returns an `IDisposable` (dispose to unsubscribe); `OnJson<T>`, `LatestJson<T>` and `HistoryJson<T>` deserialize with System.Text.Json (the non-generic `OnJson` gives a `JsonElement`). `Throttle(ch, hz)` returns an `Action<object?>`. `MembersAsync()` includes you; `ListenersAsync(ch)` returns `Declared` and `Broadcast`; `Diagnostics()` is a method. Reading state — `Latest()`, `History()`, `State`, `QueuedCount` — is thread-safe, so a UI timer can poll it.

**Pitfalls**

- **Server events** (channel messages, history, presence, remote-input holder notices) run **one at a time on the socket receive thread**. Never block there: `.Result`, `.Wait()`, `GetAwaiter().GetResult()` or `Dispatcher.Invoke` on an adapter call fails with a false `AckTimeout` after 15 s (the server did accept it — a retry publishes twice), and a callback blocked past the server's heartbeat drops the connection.
- **Lifecycle events may arrive on other threads** (the reconnect task, the thread that called `CloseAsync()`; `Dispose()` raises `Ended` synchronously on the caller's thread). Marshal UI work with `Dispatcher.BeginInvoke`/`InvokeAsync`, `SynchronizationContext.Post` or Unity's main-thread queue — never `Dispatcher.Invoke`.
- **`async` lambdas are `async void`**: wrap the body in try/catch — an escaping exception crashes the process. `await` inside them is fine (the receive thread is released at the first `await`).
- A handler that throws stops neither the adapter nor other handlers: it arrives on `Error` as `SubscriberError`. Subscribing outside a `strictRouting` declaration arrives as `StrictRoutingWarning`.
- `SendAsync`/`SendJsonAsync` throw validation errors synchronously — keep them inside `try`, not only observed through the returned `Task`.
- System.Text.Json keeps C# property names as written and matches case-sensitively: `record Target(double X)` sends `{"X":…}`. Use lowercase names (as above) or `[JsonPropertyName("x")]`.
- If you pass `ConnectOptions.HttpClient`, give every client its own: clients sharing one cookie-enabled `HttpClient` join as the **same participant**, and closing one marks the other as left.
- Options: `ExclusiveName`, `StrictRouting`, `AutoRejoin`, `AckTimeout`/`JoinTimeout` (`TimeSpan`), `UsePolling`, `OnLog`, `QueueLimit`, `OsHostname`.

## Kotlin / JVM / Android

**Install** — JVM 11+ target, from Maven Central (run Gradle on JDK 17–21). A complete consumer project (`settings.gradle.kts`, `app/build.gradle.kts`, the program in `app/src/main/kotlin/Main.kt`, run with `./gradlew run`):

```kotlin
// settings.gradle.kts
rootProject.name = "my-adapter"
include("app")

// app/build.gradle.kts
plugins {
    kotlin("jvm") version "2.1.0"
    application
}

repositories {
    mavenCentral()   // the adapter's own dependencies come from here
}

dependencies {
    implementation("com.studioxid:omni-adapter:0.1.0")
}

application {
    mainClass = "MainKt"   // the class Kotlin makes from Main.kt
}
```

**A complete program** (`Main.kt`):

```kotlin
import com.studioxid.omniadapter.*
import kotlinx.coroutines.*
import org.json.JSONObject
import kotlin.system.exitProcess

fun main(): Unit = runBlocking {
    val token = System.getenv("CONNECT_TOKEN") ?: ""
    val client = try {
        connect(ConnectOptions(
            secretKey = token, displayName = "lobby-kiosk",
            receives = listOf("kiosk.cmd", "robot.status"), sends = listOf("kiosk.status"),
        ))
    } catch (err: AdapterError) {
        System.err.println("connect failed: ${err.code}: ${err.hint ?: err.message}")
        System.err.println(formatDoctorReport(runDoctor(token)))
        exitProcess(1)
    }
    println("joined as ${client.me?.displayName}")
    // Ctrl+C and SIGTERM both run shutdown hooks: leave the stage cleanly.
    Runtime.getRuntime().addShutdownHook(Thread { runBlocking { client.close() } })

    // Lifecycle: client.events (no replay) — NOT client.on("error"), which is a channel.
    // UNDISPATCHED subscribes before launch returns; one launch per collector (collect never returns).
    val ended = CompletableDeferred<String?>()
    val lifecycle = launch(start = CoroutineStart.UNDISPATCHED) {
        client.events.collect { event ->
            when (event) {
                is ClientEvent.Failure -> System.err.println("adapter error ${event.error.code}: ${event.error.hint ?: event.error.message}")
                is ClientEvent.StateChange -> println("state: ${event.state}")
                is ClientEvent.Ended -> ended.complete(event.reason)
                else -> Unit
            }
        }
    }

    // Callbacks run on socket.io's event thread: never runBlocking a client call here — launch it.
    client.on("kiosk.cmd") { msg ->
        launch {
            try { client.send("kiosk.status", "done: ${msg.value}", ack = true) }
            catch (err: AdapterError) {
                val why = err.hint ?: err.message   // AckTimeout carries neither a hint nor more than its code
                System.err.println("kiosk.status failed: ${if (why == err.code) err.code else "${err.code}: $why"}")
            }
        }
    }
    client.onJson("robot.status") { value, _ -> println("pose: ${(value as? JSONObject)?.optJSONArray("pose")}") }
    try {
        client.sendJson("kiosk.status", mapOf("ready" to true, "screen" to 1))  // Map/List/JSONObject/JSONArray — not a data class
    } catch (err: AdapterError) {
        val why = err.hint ?: err.message
        System.err.println("send failed: ${if (why == err.code) err.code else "${err.code}: $why"}")
    }

    val reason = ended.await()   // until the session is over, or close() from the hook
    lifecycle.cancel()
    if (reason != "client-closed") {
        System.err.println("session over: $reason")
        exitProcess(1)
    }
}
```

**Types.** `StageMessage` has `channel`, `value`, `sourceParticipantId`, `timestamp`, `messageId`. `value` and `latest(ch)` are `Any?` (`String`, a `Number`, `Boolean` or `null`); `onJson`, `latestJson` and `historyJson` give `JSONObject`/`JSONArray`/primitives (org.json) — no type parameter. `on` returns a `Closeable`. `throttle(ch, hz)` takes a `Double` and returns `(Any?) -> Unit`. `members()`, `listeners(ch)` and `close()` are suspend functions; `state` is a `StateFlow<String>` (`client.state.value`), `standby` and `queuedCount` are plain properties.

**Pitfalls**

- **Callbacks run on socket.io's event thread.** `runBlocking { client.send(…, ack = true) }` there waits for an ack that this very thread must read — it fails with `AckTimeout`. `launch` it instead, and catch inside the launched coroutine (an uncaught `AdapterError` cancels its parent scope).
- **Android**: connect in `lifecycleScope` (never `runBlocking` on the main thread), switch to `Dispatchers.Main` before touching views, add the `INTERNET` permission, and allow cleartext traffic for a plain-`http://` server.
- **JVM lifetime**: a live client keeps the JVM running (while connected and while reconnecting), so a long-running adapter needs nothing extra. It lets go after `close()`, a terminal `Ended`, or a failed `connect()`. `dispose()` alone does not end the client — it only cancels its coroutines; call `close()` first.
- `close()` ends the client at the call, sends the leave and waits for the server's confirmation (at most 1 s), so it is safe in a shutdown hook (the JVM then exits with 130/143, the usual signal codes). Called from inside a channel callback it sends the leave without waiting. Each client is its own participant: the join ignores an app-wide `CookieHandler`.
- A `state`/`events` collector on `Dispatchers.Unconfined` runs on the thread that made the transition — usually that same event thread — so the callback rule applies there too: never `runBlocking` a client call that waits for the server (`runBlocking { client.send(…, ack = true) }` fails with `AckTimeout`); launch it, or collect on a real dispatcher.
- `sendJson` accepts `Map`, `List`/`Collection`, `JSONObject`, `JSONArray`, strings, numbers, booleans and `null`; anything else (a data class) throws `ValidationError`.
- Options: `exclusiveName`, `strictRouting`, `autoRejoin`, `ackTimeoutMs`/`joinTimeoutMs`, `usePolling`, `onLog`, `queueLimit`, `osHostname`.

## Swift

**Install** — Swift 6.0+ (Xcode 16+), iOS 13+/macOS 10.15+; SwiftPM resolves the repository `ProtoPie/omni-adapter-swift` (tagged `X.Y.Z` on each release):

```swift
// swift-tools-version:5.9
import PackageDescription

let package = Package(
    name: "MyAdapter",
    platforms: [.macOS(.v10_15), .iOS(.v13)],            // required
    dependencies: [.package(url: "https://github.com/ProtoPie/omni-adapter-swift", from: "0.1.0")],
    targets: [
        .executableTarget(name: "MyAdapter", dependencies: [
            .product(name: "OmniAdapter", package: "omni-adapter-swift"),   // package = the repository name
        ]),
    ]
)
```

**A complete program** (`Sources/MyAdapter/main.swift`):

```swift
import OmniAdapter
import Foundation

let token = ProcessInfo.processInfo.environment["CONNECT_TOKEN"] ?? ""
let client: ConnectClient
do {
    client = try await connect(ConnectOptions(   // argument order is fixed by the initializer
        secretKey: token,
        displayName: "ipad-wall",
        receives: ["wall.mode", "robot.status"],
        sends: ["wall.status"]
    ))
} catch let err as AdapterError {
    print("connect failed: \(err.code): \(err.hint ?? err.message)")
    print(formatDoctorReport(await runDoctor(credential: token)))
    exit(1)
}
print("joined as \(await client.me?.displayName ?? "?")")

// Ctrl+C and SIGTERM → leave cleanly (the events() loop below then sees .ended("client-closed")).
var signalSources: [DispatchSourceSignal] = []
for sig in [SIGINT, SIGTERM] {
    signal(sig, SIG_IGN)
    let source = DispatchSource.makeSignalSource(signal: sig, queue: .main)
    source.setEventHandler { Task { await client.close() } }
    source.resume()
    signalSources.append(source)
}

// Channel callbacks are synchronous, off the main actor, in arrival order.
await client.on("wall.mode") { message in
    print("wall.mode = \(message.value.stringValue ?? "-")")   // print(message.value) shows string("…")
}
await client.onJSON("robot.status") { value, _ in   // value: [String: Any], [Any], String, NSNumber…
    if let status = value as? [String: Any], let pose = status["pose"] as? [Double] { print("pose: \(pose)") }
}

let brightness = 0.8
do {
    try await client.send("wall.status", "ready", ack: true)
    try await client.send("wall.status", .double(brightness))   // variables need the enum case
    try await client.sendJSON("wall.status", ["screen": 1, "on": true])
} catch let err as AdapterError {
    let why = err.hint ?? err.message   // AckTimeout carries neither a hint nor more than its code
    print("send failed: \(why == err.code ? err.code : "\(err.code): \(why)")")
}

// Lifecycle: client.events() — NOT client.on("error"), which is a channel.
for await event in await client.events() {
    switch event {
    case .failure(let err): print("adapter error \(err.code): \(err.hint ?? err.message)")
    case .stateChange(let state): print("state: \(state.rawValue)")
    case .ended(let reason):                                    // the last event
        await client.close()   // lets the leave started by the signal handler finish (a no-op otherwise)
        if reason != "client-closed" { print("session over: \(reason ?? "ended")") }
        exit(reason == "client-closed" ? 0 : 1)
    default: break
    }
}
```

**Types.** `StageMessage` has `channel`, `value`, `sourceParticipantId`, `timestamp`, `messageId`. `value` and `latest(ch)` are the `Primitive` enum (`.string`, `.int`, `.double`, `.bool`, `.null`): read with `.stringValue`/`.doubleValue`/`.boolValue`/`.jsonValue` (interpolating the raw value prints `string("go")`); literals convert automatically, variables need the case (`.double(x)`). A prototype's value arrives as `.string("42")` — `.doubleValue` is `nil` for it; parse with `Double(value.stringValue ?? "")`. `onJSON`, `latestJSON` and `historyJSON` give `Any` (`JSONSerialization` types; a JSON `null` arrives as `NSNull`). `on` returns a `Subscription` — it is **not** cancelled on deinit; call `cancel()`. `throttle(ch, hz:)` returns a synchronous `(Primitive) throws -> Void` — call it with `try push(.double(x))`; it checks the channel there (the value is already type-safe). `members()` and `listeners(ch)` are `async throws`; `state` is a `TransportState` enum (`.rawValue` for the string).

**Pitfalls**

- `ConnectClient` is an `actor`: every call is `await`ed (`try await` where it throws), properties included (`await client.standby`). `close()` ends the client at the call and waits up to 1 s for the leave to be confirmed. Each client carries its own guest cookie, so two clients in one app are two participants.
- **Callbacks are synchronous, off the main actor, in arrival order.** Hop to UI with `Task { @MainActor in … }` (you cannot `await MainActor.run` inside a synchronous callback); hand heavy work to a `Task` — a slow callback delays the ones behind it. Past 1000 waiting messages the oldest skip their callback (`latest()` stays exact; the ring records `queue-overflow` with `inbound:`).
- `ConnectOptions(...)` takes its arguments in initializer order (`secretKey, url, stageId, displayName, osHostname, receives, sends, providesView, strictRouting`). Set the rest as properties: `var options = ConnectOptions(secretKey: token); options.exclusiveName = true` (also `autoRejoin`, `ackTimeout`, `joinTimeout`, `usePolling`, `onLog`, `queueLimit`).
- `sendJSON` takes what `JSONSerialization` can encode (`[String: Any]`, `[Any]`, strings, numbers, booleans); anything else throws `ValidationError`.
- Apps: a plain-`http://` server addressed by host name needs an App Transport Security exception (the join's HTTP request goes through `URLSession`; a command-line tool is not affected); a sandboxed macOS app needs the `com.apple.security.network.client` entitlement. `throttle(hz:)` with `hz <= 0` traps (precondition); the other languages throw `ConfigError`.

## Dart / Flutter

**Install** — Dart 3.4+, Flutter incl. web; `dart pub add omni_adapter` (Flutter: `flutter pub add omni_adapter`), or in `pubspec.yaml`:

```yaml
dependencies:
  omni_adapter: ^0.1.0
```

**A complete program** (`bin/main.dart`, Dart VM):

```dart
import 'dart:async';
import 'dart:io';

import 'package:omni_adapter/omni_adapter.dart';

Future<void> main() async {
  final token = Platform.environment['CONNECT_TOKEN'] ?? '';
  final ConnectClient client;
  try {
    client = await connect(ConnectOptions(
      secretKey: token,
      displayName: 'line3-monitor',
      receives: const ['line3.temp', 'robot.status'],
      sends: const ['line3.ack'],
    ));
  } on AdapterError catch (err) {
    stderr.writeln('connect failed: ${err.code}: ${err.hint ?? err.message}');
    stderr.writeln(formatDoctorReport(await runDoctor(token)));
    exit(1);
  }
  print('joined as ${client.me?.displayName}');
  // Ctrl+C and SIGTERM → leave cleanly (SIGTERM cannot be watched on Windows).
  final signals = [
    ProcessSignal.sigint,
    if (!Platform.isWindows) ProcessSignal.sigterm,
  ].map((s) => s.watch().listen((_) => client.close())).toList();

  // Lifecycle: onEvent(name, …) — NOT on('error'), which is a channel. Payloads are Object?.
  final ended = Completer<String?>();
  client.onEvent('error', (e) {
    final err = e as AdapterError;
    stderr.writeln('adapter error ${err.code}: ${err.hint ?? err.message}');
  });
  client.onEvent('stateChange', (state) => print('state: $state')); // a String
  client.onEvent('memberJoin', (m) => print('+ ${(m as Member).displayName}'));
  client.onEvent('memberLeave', (participantId) => print('- $participantId'));
  client.onEvent('ended', (reason) {
    if (!ended.isCompleted) ended.complete(reason as String?);
  });

  client.on('line3.*', (msg) => print('${msg.channel} = ${msg.value}'));
  // value: the decoded JSON — Map, List, num, String, bool or null.
  client.onJson('robot.status', (value) => print('status: $value'));

  try {
    // send/sendJson throw validation errors SYNCHRONOUSLY — keep them inside try.
    await client.send('line3.ack', true, ack: true);
    await client.sendJson('line3.ack', {'ok': true, 'count': 1});
  } on AdapterError catch (err) {
    final why = err.hint ?? err.message; // AckTimeout carries neither a hint nor more than its code
    stderr.writeln('send failed: ${why == err.code ? err.code : '${err.code}: $why'}');
  }

  final reason = await ended.future;
  for (final s in signals) {
    await s.cancel();
  }
  if (reason != 'client-closed') {
    stderr.writeln('session over: $reason');
    exit(1);
  }
}
```

**In a Flutter widget:**

```dart
import 'dart:async';

import 'package:omni_adapter/omni_adapter.dart';
import 'package:flutter/material.dart';

class Panel extends StatefulWidget {
  const Panel({super.key});
  @override
  State<Panel> createState() => _PanelState();
}

class _PanelState extends State<Panel> {
  // --dart-define=CONNECT_TOKEN=cst_… — compiled into the app (see pitfalls).
  static const _token = String.fromEnvironment('CONNECT_TOKEN');
  ConnectClient? _client;
  String _text = 'connecting…';

  @override
  void initState() {
    super.initState();
    unawaited(_join());
  }

  Future<void> _join() async {
    try {
      final client = await connect(ConnectOptions(
          secretKey: _token,
          displayName: 'flutter-panel',
          receives: const ['panel.value']));
      if (!mounted) {
        unawaited(client.close()); // the widget went away while connecting: free the seat
        return;
      }
      _client = client;
      client.on('panel.value', (msg) {
        if (mounted) setState(() => _text = '${msg.value}');
      });
    } on AdapterError catch (err) {
      if (mounted) setState(() => _text = err.hint ?? err.message);
    }
  }

  @override
  void dispose() {
    unawaited(_client?.close()); // dispose() is synchronous: never await here
    super.dispose();
  }

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) => Text(_text);
}
```

**Types.** `StageMessage` has `channel`, `value`, `sourceParticipantId`, `timestamp`, `messageId`; `value` and `latest(ch)` are `Object?` (`Primitive` is a typedef for it, so a non-primitive compiles and then throws `ValidationError`). `on` and `onEvent` return an unsubscribe function; lifecycle payloads are `Object?` — cast them (`e as AdapterError`, `m as Member`). `state` is a `TransportState` enum, while the `stateChange` payload is its name as a `String`. `throttle(ch, hz: 10)`.

**Pitfalls**

- **`send`/`sendJson` throw validation errors (bad value, closed client, unencodable JSON) synchronously** — not as a `Future` error: `catchError` and `unawaited` do not catch them. Call them inside `try`.
- Callbacks run synchronously in the zone you called `connect()` from; heavy work in one janks the UI.
- **Flutter tokens**: `--dart-define=CONNECT_TOKEN=cst_…` values are **compiled into the app** (in a Flutter web build they are plain text in `main.dart.js`, readable by every visitor) — use a token you are ready to revoke. Read it with `const String.fromEnvironment('CONNECT_TOKEN')`; never `Platform.environment` (dart:io) on the web.
- `dispose()` is synchronous: `unawaited(_client?.close());` then `super.dispose()`. Guard `setState` after any `await` with `mounted`, and close a client whose `connect` finished after `dispose()` (`!mounted` right after the `await`) — both shown above.
- Platforms: a sandboxed macOS app (Flutter macOS included) needs the `com.apple.security.network.client` entitlement; Android needs `INTERNET`. On native platforms the adapter uses `dart:io` sockets, which App Transport Security does not govern — a macOS build reached a plain-`http://` host with no exception (not verified on iOS). `usePolling: true` works on Flutter web only.
- `osHostname` is filled in automatically on the Dart VM (the only language that does). Options: `exclusiveName`, `strictRouting`, `autoRejoin`, `ackTimeout`/`joinTimeout` (`Duration`), `onLog`, `logger`, `queueLimit`.

## Errors and troubleshooting

Every failure is an `AdapterError` with a stable `code` (branch on it), a `message`, and usually a `hint` — a one-line next step. Print the code and the hint, falling back to the message: TS/Swift/Dart `err.hint ?? err.message` · Python `err.hint or err.message` · C# `err.Hint ?? err.Message` · Kotlin `err.hint ?: err.message`. When an error has no message of its own, the message is the code itself (`AckTimeout` prints as `AckTimeout`) — so also say which call failed, as the programs above do. Errors throw from the call that caused them; errors that happen later arrive on the error event.

| Code | Meaning | What to do |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ConfigError` | Bad options or credential, before any network call: unset or empty token, whitespace around it, a bare `ck_` without `url`/`stageId`, an empty `receives`/`sends` list | Follow the hint. Bare `ck_`: use the `cst_` token instead |
| `RoomEnded` | No live session | `connect()` fails with it at once. Open the stage in Connect, or use a key created with **Let adapters start a session** turned on (Share → Adapter keys — a key keeps the setting it was issued with) so it can start one. After a successful join, a session that closes is waited out by `autoRejoin` instead |
| `AuthRevoked` | Key revoked or expired, or issued for another stage or server — or the stage is closed to guests (`stage-locked`) | Create a new key. Stage locked: adapters join as guests; ask the stage owner or whoever runs your Connect to reopen the stage to guests |
| `StageFull` | Participant cap reached (each connection is one seat) | Stop clients you do not need; reuse one client |
| `StageArchived` | The stage is archived | Ask an Editor or Owner to restore it |
| `NotConnected` | Server unreachable — or `members()`/`listeners()` called while the client is not connected (reconnecting, closing), or `ensureStreamLayer()` got a server error (5xx) or no answer within the ack timeout | Check the network or VPN; re-copy the token if the server moved. From a roster call or `ping()`, the hint names the case: not joined yet (wait for connect), reconnecting (call again once `connected`, then re-read `members()`), or ended (create a new client) |
| `JoinTimeout` | Reached the server, never admitted — often a proxy blocking WebSocket | Force long-polling: TS `transports: ['polling']` · Python `transports=["polling"]` · C# `UsePolling = true` · Kotlin/Swift `usePolling = true` · Dart `usePolling: true` (Flutter web only) |
| `ProtocolVersionMismatch` / `ClientAheadOfServer` | Adapter and server speak incompatible protocol versions | Update the older side |
| `ValidationError` | A bad channel or value (from the call), or the server rejected the join body (usually a version skew; the message names the fields) | Fix the value; for a join rejection update the older side |
| `SessionEnded` | The client was closed or the session is over (a queued acked send that already went out once before a drop may still have reached the server) | Build a new client |
| `AckTimeout` | No server ack within the ack timeout | The server may still have the message — do not blindly retry |
| `Standby` | An `ack: true` send while another instance of an `exclusiveName` is active, or a queued acked send discarded when this instance became standby (which the server may already have, if it went out once before a drop) | Expected for a standby copy |
| `QueueOverflow` | The full queue dropped this acked send (oldest first) — if it had already gone out once before a drop, the server may still have it | Send less — under 60 messages a second, and less while disconnected — or change `queueLimit` |
| `TooManyRequests` | The server's rate limit (60 messages a second per connection), seen on acked sends — and thrown by `ensureStreamLayer()` on a 429, and by `connect()` when the server refuses the join: too many failed join attempts from this network address (20 within 5 minutes — usually another program here still using a revoked or mistyped token), or more than 60 joins a minute with one adapter key (a restart loop); servers without the per-key join limit also refuse a sixth join from one address within a minute. From `connect()` the error carries `retryAfterMs` — the server's remaining window: up to 5 minutes for the address cap, up to 60 s for the per-key limit, 1 s when the server is validating more than 200 joins at once — and the hint says the seconds; while rejoining, the adapter waits at least that long before the next attempt | Sends: nothing — the adapter backs off and re-sends from the queue by itself (not thrown); coalesce high-rate sources with `throttle()`. `ensureStreamLayer()`: retry later. `connect()`: not retried — wait up to 5 minutes and fix the program with the old token |
| `KeyMaterialUnavailable` | `connect()` only (503): the server cannot read the stored material of an adapter key on the stage. Each such attempt alone fails with a plain 500 (`Internal`, no hint); after 30 of them from one address within a minute for one stage every key — a correct one too — gets this 503 until the minute ends. The error carries `retryAfterMs` (the rest of that minute) | `connect()`: not retried — the hint says what to ask of whoever runs your Connect (revoke the stage's old keys or restore the key material); a joined client keeps retrying while it rejoins, waiting at least `retryAfterMs` |
| `Unauthorized` · `NotSupported` | The server refused a roster request (for example this connection was already marked as left) · the call is not available here (a remote-input registration on the Engine profile, `ensureStreamLayer()` on a server without the route — its other errors are listed under the screen broadcast section) | Reconnect with a fresh client · check `docs/COMPATIBILITY.md` and the hint |
| `SubscriberError` · `StrictRoutingWarning` | On the error event: one of your handlers threw (C#, Kotlin; elsewhere it is logged) · a subscription outside the `strictRouting` declaration (C#, Kotlin, Swift; TS/Python/Dart log a warning) | Fix the handler · the declaration |

### Doctor

Run it before debugging code — it checks the token, the URL shape, the server, screen and remote-input support, the live session and a real join, and names the failing step with a fix. Only `✖` lines need fixing; `△` and `·` are information. It diagnoses a `cst_` token (wrap a bare `ck_` key, or use the issued token). It also tells a server that takes no adapters at all (a Connect without adapter support) from a revoked key, and warns when the key inside the token is not 46 characters long (a truncated or altered copy — such a key is refused with a 401, and `connect()`'s hint says the same).

```bash
npx --no-install omni-adapter doctor "$CONNECT_TOKEN"   # in a Node project that installed the adapter
omni-adapter doctor "$CONNECT_TOKEN"                    # Python environment (or: python -m omni_adapter doctor …)
omni-adapter doctor "$CONNECT_TOKEN" --json             # CheckResult[] for scripts; exit code 1 if any check failed
```

Every language also has it as a library call (see the [name map](#name-map)); each complete program above prints the report when `connect` fails.

### Connected but nothing happens

1. Still connected, backlog empty? Read `state` and `queuedCount`. A backlog while `connected` means sending is held back: you send faster than 60 messages a second (`queue-overflow` in the ring once it is full), or a `TooManyRequests` backoff (no `send-dropped` in the ring, not standby), or the server is not acking a queued acked send (nothing is recorded for that; the adapter keeps the item and retries it by itself). A fire-and-forget send the server refuses — direct or queued — leaves no trace at all; send with `ack: true` while you debug.
2. Read `diagnostics()` — the last 100 lifecycle points, recorded even if you subscribed to nothing.
3. Does anyone receive the channel? Call `listeners(channel)` once: `declared` and `broadcast` both empty means nobody does — a typo, or the peer is not up. `declared` empty but `broadcast` non-empty is normal when the receiver is a prototype (prototypes never declare).
4. With `strictRouting: true`, only exact declared `receives` arrive.
5. Watch the channel from a second connection: `omni-adapter watch "$CONNECT_TOKEN" 'line3.*' --count 1 --timeout 5`. It exits 0 even when nothing arrived — count its output lines to judge liveness.
6. Your own messages never come back to you (no self-echo) — test with a second client or the Console.

## Roster, diagnostics, testing, CLI

**Roster.** `members()` returns everyone in the session, **including you**. Presence is event-driven: use the join/leave events instead of polling — but **re-read `members()` after every (re)connect** (when the state becomes `connected`): joins and leaves that happened while you were disconnected are not replayed as events. A `Member` has `participantId` (don't store it — it can change when the client rejoins, e.g. after the server's guest token expires; `me` always holds your current one, updated before each `connected`) and `displayName` (the stable name), plus optional fields that are **absent** when not declared or on older servers: `clientType` (`'adapter'` = this library, `'player'` = a ProtoPie player, absent = a browser), `receives`/`sends` (absent = declared nothing, not "deaf"), `strictRouting`, `exclusiveName`, `standby` (absent = active), `osHostname` (which machine — set it yourself, automatic only on the Dart VM; blank values are dropped) and `providesView` (`'none' | 'web' | 'stream'`). Python uses snake_case fields, C# PascalCase. `listeners(channel)` takes an exact channel name and returns `{ channel, declared, broadcast }` — two lists of `Member`: those whose `receives` match, and those that receive it without declaring it — you excluded. It costs one `members()` round trip — call it at wiring time or from a diagnostics screen, not per message. Both are server round trips and reject with `NotConnected` while the client is not connected (reconnecting, or closing) — call them on `connected`. Signatures: TS `await client.members()` → `Member[]`, `await client.listeners(ch)` → `Listeners`; Python `await client.members()` → `list[Member]`, `await client.listeners(ch)` → `Listeners` (`declared`/`broadcast` are tuples); C# `await client.MembersAsync()` → `IReadOnlyList<Member>`, `await client.ListenersAsync(ch)` → `Listeners` (`Declared`/`Broadcast`); Kotlin `client.members()` → `List<Member>`, `client.listeners(ch)` → `Listeners` (both suspend); Swift `try await client.members()` → `[Member]`, `try await client.listeners(ch)` → `Listeners`; Dart `await client.members()` → `List<Member>`, `await client.listeners(ch)` → `Listeners`. The roster says a socket is joined, not that the peer's process is doing its job: for liveness, have the peer publish a periodic tick and watch it.

**Diagnostics ring.** `diagnostics()` returns the last 100 entries `{ at, level, code, message }`, recorded with no setup and never containing a credential. Stream them into your logger with the `onLog` option; add your own marks with `note(code, message, level)`.

**Console output by default.** TypeScript prints warnings and errors to the console as `[omni-adapter] …` (debug lines only with `debug: true`); pass `logger: (level, message) => …` to redirect them, or `logger: () => {}` to silence them. Python logs through the standard `logging` logger `omni_adapter` — its warnings reach stderr until you configure logging (`logging.getLogger("omni_adapter").setLevel(logging.ERROR)` quiets it). Dart prints every line, debug included, as `[omni-adapter] …` unless you pass `logger: (level, message) {}`. C#, Kotlin and Swift print nothing — use `OnLog`/`onLog` or read `diagnostics()`.

| code | meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `state` · `ended` · `error` | state change · session over (with reason) · server or transport error (recorded even with no subscriber) |
| `send-dropped` | the server rejected an acked send; fire-and-forget sends (direct or queued) are never acknowledged, so their rejection is not seen |
| `queue-overflow` | the queue is full and drops its oldest items — noted once per episode, again only after it drained to half its limit (Swift also: `inbound:` skipped callbacks) |
| `standby` · `active` | exclusiveName judgment changed (`— dropped N queued sends` when becoming standby discarded the queue) |
| `no-listener` | written only by a `listeners()` call when nobody declared the channel — `warn` if nobody receives it at all, `info` if undeclared receivers exist |
| `input-channel` · `hello` · `input-dropped` | remote input (see Optional) |
| `engine-channels` | Web View: a declared channel is outside the layer's Stage messages rule for its direction (Receive for `receives`, Send for `sends`) |

**Testing without a server — `MemoryStage`** (all six): an in-process stage with the same rules (no self-echo, strict routing, history re-seed on join and reconnect, exclusiveName judgment); no credential, no doctor, no screens, and no 60-messages-a-second limit (its transport sets `bypassRateLimit` — `bypass_rate_limit` in Python, `IRateLimitBypassTransport` in C#; Dart's client recognises `MemoryTransport` itself).

```ts
import { MemoryStage } from '@studioxid/omni-adapter';

export async function aTriggersB(): Promise<number[]> {
  const stage = new MemoryStage();   // options: roomId, historyLimit, rejectPublish (failure injection), now
  const sensor = await stage.join({ displayName: 'line-sensor', sends: ['line.temp'] });
  const alarm = await stage.join({ displayName: 'alarm-panel', receives: ['line.temp'], strictRouting: true });
  const seen: number[] = [];
  alarm.on('line.temp', (msg) => seen.push(Number(msg.value)));
  await sensor.send('line.temp', 91);           // A triggers B
  stage.inject('line.temp', 42);                // as if a prototype sent it
  await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 0));   // delivery lands on the next tick
  stage.disconnect(alarm); stage.reconnect(alarm);   // reproduce a drop
  stage.end();                                  // everyone gets 'ended'
  return seen;                                  // [91, 42]
}
```

Names: TS `stage.join({ … })`; Python `await stage.join(display_name=…)`; Kotlin `stage.join(MemoryJoinOptions(…))`; Swift `try await stage.join(MemoryJoinOptions(…))`; Dart `await stage.join(MemoryJoinOptions(…))`; C# `await stage.JoinAsync(new MemoryJoinOptions { … })`.

**Testing without hardware** (all six): `replay(client, parseRecording(text), { speed: 2, loop: 1 })` re-publishes a recording (the NDJSON that `omni-adapter record`/`watch` write) with its original gaps ÷ `speed`; `simulate(client, 'line.temp', { waveform: 'sine', min: 18, max: 26, hz: 2, durationMs: 30_000 })` emits synthetic values (`'sine' | 'ramp' | 'random' | 'step'`). Both publish through `send()` — rate limit, queue, standby and backoff rules apply — wait for the queue to drain (giving up after 15 s without progress) before returning, stop on `ended` or when cancelled, and return the partial count.

**Latency and repro bundles.** `ping()` times one server round trip without publishing anything; `measureLatency` gives min/p50/p95/max over 10 samples — adapter↔server only, not end-to-end (TS/Python `measureLatency(client)` / `measure_latency(client)`; Kotlin `measureLatency({ client.ping() })`; Swift `try await measureLatency(ping: { try await client.ping() })`; Dart `measureLatency(client.ping)`; C# `Latency.MeasureAsync(client.PingAsync)`). A repro bundle carries diagnostics, doctor results and the server's version info with only a fingerprint of the credential — pass the live client's diagnostics or its list stays empty: TS `buildReport(credential, { diagnostics: client.diagnostics() })`, Python `build_report(credential, diagnostics=…)`, Dart `buildReport(credential, diagnostics: …)`, Kotlin `Report.build(credential, diagnostics = …)`, Swift `try await Report.build(credential: …, diagnostics: …)`, C# `Report.BuildAsync(credential, diagnostics: …)`.

**CLI** (TypeScript and Python packages; the credential comes first):

```bash
omni-adapter doctor   "$CONNECT_TOKEN" [--json]
omni-adapter send     "$CONNECT_TOKEN" door.open true                  # acked; exit 0/1
omni-adapter send     "$CONNECT_TOKEN" robot.status '{"x":1}' --json   # JSON convention
omni-adapter watch    "$CONNECT_TOKEN" 'line3.*' --count 5 --timeout 30   # NDJSON {ts, channel, value, from}
omni-adapter watch    "$CONNECT_TOKEN" --history                       # include the replay backlog
omni-adapter record   "$CONNECT_TOKEN" 'sensor.*' --out run.ndjson --timeout 60
omni-adapter replay   "$CONNECT_TOKEN" run.ndjson --speed 2
omni-adapter simulate "$CONNECT_TOKEN" sensor.temperature --sine 18..26 --hz 2 --seconds 30
```

**Examples.** Every language has three runnable common examples — quickstart, bidirectional + roster, resilience (reconnect, offline queue, auto-rejoin). The npm and NuGet packages ship them under `examples/` (paths from the package root):

- npm: `examples/01-quickstart.ts` · `02-sensor-bridge.ts` · `03-operations-console.ts`, plus `_shared.ts` (the credential helper they import). Node does not run TypeScript from inside `node_modules`: copy the example and `_shared.ts` into the project, change `'../dist/index.js'` to `'@studioxid/omni-adapter'` in both, and run it with Node 22.18+ (`node 01-quickstart.ts "$CONNECT_TOKEN"`) or `npx tsx`.
- NuGet: `examples/Quickstart/Program.cs` · `RosterBridge/Program.cs` · `Resilience/Program.cs` — each is the whole program of a `dotnet new console` app with the package added.

## Optional

Screens are experimental and need a recent Connect server — check `docs/COMPATIBILITY.md` (in the npm and NuGet packages, and at that path in the adapter repository) before relying on them. The full guide is `skills/using-omni-adapter/references/screens-and-remote-input.md` (same places).

### Declaring a screen (`providesView`)

`providesView: 'none'` (default — data only) · `'web'` — the adapter's screen is a web page (a **Web View** layer shows a page by its URL, not by adapter name) · `'stream'` — the adapter renders and broadcasts its own screen into an **Adapter Stream** layer. The Adapter Stream layer finds the adapter by `displayName`, so keep it stable. Declaring does not make a picture appear — the layer shows "waiting" until the adapter streams. `doctor` reports whether the server accepts `providesView` (an older server strips it silently) and whether remote input exists on the server.

### Web View and the Engine profile

In Connect Omni, a **Web View** layer (Add → Web View: the page URL) embeds your page and hands it a `MessagePort` — every Web View does, there is no switch — so the page exchanges stage messages **without a credential and without a seat**. What passes is set on the layer, in its property panel's **Stage messages** section: **Receive** (the channels the page may receive) and **Send** (the channels it may send on), up to 32 exact names each, no wildcards; empty rules pass nothing. In TypeScript, `connect()` with no credential inside that iframe takes this Engine profile automatically — call it during page start-up, before awaiting anything else (the port arrives once, at the iframe's load event). Dart (Flutter web) and C# (Blazor WebAssembly) build an `EngineTransport` explicitly, and the Engine-only controls live on `EngineTransport` there, not on the client. `receives` and `sends` must list exact channel names (no wildcards — the port delivers only what is subscribed, and the host drops a whole send declaration when one name holds a pattern or is not 1–512 characters, so the adapter rejects those with `ConfigError`). Declare every channel the page uses (rule 11): `receives` goes to the host as the subscription and `sends` as a declaration (`engine:message-declare` — Connect Omni hosts from 2026-10-27 on; older ones ignore it), so Connect knows the page's channels before any message flows. On Connect Omni hosts from 2026-11-05, the declared channels are turned on in the layer's Receive and Send rules automatically when an editor's screen displays the page (a viewer's screen does not save rules); a channel an editor turned off stays off. What is not declared — a send the rules refused, a wildcard, names past 32 — appears in that Web View's Stage messages as "This page asked for", only in the editor displaying the page, and the designer adds it with **Add**. On older hosts every declared channel waits there for **Add**. Backstage draws the declared channels the rules allow as chips on that layer's node. With empty rules the page still connects and its requests reach the editor, but nothing flows until its channels are turned on (an editor opening the page, or **Add**) (Connect Omni hosts before 2026-10-27 hand over no port, so `connect()` ends in `JoinTimeout`). A `receives` entry outside the Receive rules never arrives and a send outside the Send rules is refused by the host — TypeScript notes each as `engine-channels` in `diagnostics()`. The layer's rules are readable for comparison: `client.engine.allowedReceives` / `allowedSends` in TypeScript, `allowedReceives` / `allowedSends` (Dart) and `AllowedReceives` / `AllowedSends` (C#) on `EngineTransport`; `allowedChannels` (both directions together) is deprecated. Saving changed rules reloads the page with a new port. There is no history ring, `members()` is empty and there is no `sendTo`; `latest()` works (the host replays each subscribed channel's last value). In TypeScript `client.engine` adds a presenter lease (`acquireControl`), shared state (`setState`/`onState`, ≤ 8 KB) and session snapshots (≤ 512 KB).

### Broadcasting a screen
