The helper owns the signalling (announce on every connect, answer each viewer's offer, ICE relay, cleanup when viewers leave or the client ends); you supply the media — one WebRTC session per viewer from the stack you already use. No language adds a media dependency.

```ts
import { connect, startScreenBroadcast } from '@studioxid/omni-adapter';

export async function broadcastCanvas(token: string, canvas: HTMLCanvasElement): Promise<void> {
  // providesView: 'stream' — the server creates and binds my Adapter Stream layer when I join
  const client = await connect({ secretKey: token, displayName: 'my-simulator', providesView: 'stream' });
  console.log('layer name:', client.me?.displayName);   // the name the server gave me — may be 'my-simulator (2)'
  const broadcast = startScreenBroadcast({
    client,
    stream: canvas.captureStream(30),
    onRemoteInput: (msg) => console.log(msg.t, msg.x, msg.y),   // pointer: down|move|up|cancel, x/y in [0,1]
  });
  console.log(broadcast.viewerCount);   // broadcast.stop() ends it early
}
```

| Language | Start | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Python | `await start_screen_broadcast(client, create_session=open_session, on_remote_input=…)` | `aiortc` via the `[stream]` extra; a 4-parameter factory `(viewer, send_ice, ice_servers, wire_input)` receives the input channel |
| C# | `ScreenBroadcast.Start(client, createSession, onError, onRemoteInput)` | one `IBroadcastSession` per viewer; use the 3- or 4-parameter factory to receive the ICE servers; stop with `Dispose()`; the Unity example is the reference |
| Kotlin | `startScreenBroadcast(client, createSession = { viewer, sendIce, iceServers, wireInput -> … })` | pass the factory **by name** — a trailing lambda binds to the last parameter (`scope`) |
| Swift | `await startScreenBroadcast(client: client, createSession: { viewer, sendIce, iceServers, wireInput in … })` | |
| Dart | `startScreenBroadcast(client: client, createSession: (viewer, sendIce, iceServers, wireInput) async => …)` | `flutter_webrtc` lives in your app |

- **ICE servers come from the server**: every language has `fetchIceServers()` (STUN + short-lived TURN; successes are cached, failures are not — the next call asks again. On failure it returns a still-cached list (one due for refresh — lists are fetched again at half their remaining lifetime), else the server's public STUN list when only the stage's list failed, else `[]`). The TS helper applies it; elsewhere hand it to your peer configuration. A peer built without it connects inside the same network only ("works in the office, remote viewers see nothing"). Do not hard-code STUN URLs.
- **The layer comes from `providesView: 'stream'`**: on a server with adapter stream layers, an adapter that joins with it gets its Adapter Stream layer created and bound by the server — in the first group placed on the stage, matched by the name the server gave it (`client.me.displayName`); a deleted layer comes back on the next join. Without the declaration no layer is created and the helper records `stream-undeclared` once in `diagnostics()`.
- `ensureStreamLayer()` (Python `ensure_stream_layer()`) is optional — an idempotent call that returns that layer. `renamed: true` means the server gave you another name than you asked for (`name (2)`): another program on a different key uses this name, or you rotated keys without revoking the old one (a screen adapter's layer stays bound to the old key) — rename one, or revoke the old key; a layer under the original name will not show you. TypeScript, Python and Dart log a warning; all six expose `renamed`. Errors: 404 `NotSupported` (server too old), `RoomEnded` (no live session), 429 `TooManyRequests`, `ValidationError` with the server's message (not declared `providesView: 'stream'`, or too many Adapter Stream layers — the hint says which), `NotConnected` (5xx, network, ack timeout, or a server failure while re-validating the key after a 401), `SessionEnded` after `close()`; any other error of that re-validation passes through as `connect()` would report it (for example `AuthRevoked` for a revoked key).
- When the stream source starts or changes after the helper started — not per frame — call `sourceChanged()` (Python `source_changed()`, C# `SourceChanged()`): it re-announces the adapter so viewers whose offer went unanswered offer again. Calls are coalesced to at most one announcement per second (the first call, then one at the end of the window if more came in); Python's is safe from any thread.
- **Old sessions are closed for you**: when the adapter comes back with a new participant id (a rejoin into a new session, the 6-hour guest-token revalidation), the viewer sessions from before the drop are closed — viewers address the adapter by participant id and offer again (sessions a viewer opened to the new id while the adapter was still reconnecting stay).
- **Early viewer ICE is queued**: candidates that arrive while the connection is being set up are applied once the offer is set (no age limit); candidates that arrive before the offer wait up to 10 s, matched by `negotiationId` — at most 200 per receiver, 4 waiting receivers per viewer and 64 in all (`ice-queue` in `diagnostics()` when something is dropped). The ICE-server lookup gives up after 5 s and uses the last known servers; a failed lookup is never cached, so the next viewer asks again (`ice-servers`).
- **One session per viewer receiver**: the web keeps one receiver per (viewer page × adapter participant) — not per layer instance (two layers on one page that show this adapter share it) — and tags offers and ICE with its `receiverId`, so two tabs of the same PIN guest are two sessions instead of closing each other's. A new offer replaces only that receiver's session; `peer-left` closes every session of that participant; answers and ICE echo `negotiationId` and `receiverId`. Your session factory runs once per receiver (the same participant id twice) and `viewerCount` counts receivers. A viewer without `receiverId` (older web) keeps one session per participant. A participant keeps at most 4 receiver sessions. A fifth evicts first a session the helper knows is not live (TypeScript: its connection is not `connected`; where the app injects sessions: a receiver whose session has not sent its answer yet — an answered session stays live while it renegotiates), then the least recently negotiated one. Until a vanished tab is noticed — ICE takes seconds to report it, and an injected session only once the app passes it to `session_closed`/`sessionClosed` — a live tab that never renegotiates can be the one evicted, so report closures. Only PIN and share-link guests keep their participant id across a refresh and so leave old receivers behind; team members get a new id per socket and leave with `peer-left`. The TS helper also closes a session whose `RTCPeerConnection` goes `failed` or `closed`; where you inject the session, report that by passing it back — `broadcast.session_closed(session)` (Python, any thread), `SessionClosed(session)` (C#), `sessionClosed(session)` (Kotlin, Swift, Dart); an unknown or already replaced session is ignored.
- If you drive `stage:signaling` yourself: send `{"kind":"ready"}` on every connect (reconnects included) or late viewers never find you, and use `addTrack(track, stream)` with a stream or the viewer gets no picture. Once the client has ended (from the moment `close()` is called, or the session ends), signaling sends are dropped silently — nothing reaches the viewers.
- The picture is encoded once per viewer receiver — fine for small reviews (5–10 viewers).

### Remote input

An Editor viewing a broadcast screen can operate it with their pointer over a peer-to-peer `coc.input` data channel. **No code is needed beyond `onRemoteInput`:** the stage arms remote input for Editors as soon as the screen streams — no registration code. Connect Omni servers send lease-holder notices (key adapters are registered automatically on join and told the holder): input is accepted only from the Editor holding the lease — the Connect editor claims it automatically on the first pointer-down — and PIN or share-link viewers never control. Older servers that predate the notices never announce a holder; then the helpers' gate stays permissive and accepts every viewer's input. `submitRegistrationCode`, `resumeRegistration` and `onRemoteInputHolder` exist for registration-code deployments and are not needed otherwise. The helper whitelists directions, clamps `x`/`y` to `[0,1]` (top-left origin, no y-flip), validates pointer ids, synthesizes `cancel` when the holder changes, and re-sends `hello` every 10 s (a viewer whose tab went to the background recovers only through that). Only pointers exist — tap, drag, swipe, on-screen keyboards; no physical-keyboard input. Feed local and remote pointers through the same hit-test path. For a vehicle, block new `down`/`move` while moving but always let `up`/`cancel` through. Diagnose "operating does nothing" with the ring codes `input-channel` (channel opened), `hello` (sent) and `input-dropped` (frames discarded by the gate). References: `typescript/examples/13-driver-console.ts`, `python/examples/05_roadside_sign.py`, `dart/example_aaos`.

### Unity

`csharp/examples/Unity` in the adapter repository (Unity 2021.3 LTS; not in the NuGet package) is the reference: it ships the main-thread dispatcher, a lifecycle `MonoBehaviour` and `fetch-plugins.sh`. Not supported: WebGL. Not verified: IL2CPP. UPM packaging is not done — copy the **whole** dependency closure into `Assets/Plugins/` (Unity drops a plugin whose references it cannot resolve).

- Callbacks arrive on the socket thread: marshal to the main thread before touching any Unity API; never block in a callback. Sends throw validation errors synchronously — wrap them in `try`.
- Close the client in `OnDestroy`/`OnApplicationQuit` (`Dispose()` leaves without waiting).

For a Unity screen broadcast, four things fail silently:

1. Set `Application.runInBackground = true` — otherwise the frame loop (and the `WebRTC.Update()` pump) stops whenever the operator focuses the browser, and the connection drops after a few seconds.
2. IMGUI (`OnGUI`) never reaches the broadcast; put stage-visible UI on a `Canvas` in `ScreenSpaceCamera` mode bound to the broadcast camera.
3. The broadcast camera is the one with a `targetTexture`, not necessarily `Camera.main`.
4. `RTCDataChannel.Send` throws before the channel is open, and `OnDataChannel` usually fires while it is still connecting — queue until `OnOpen`.

### Android Automotive (AAOS) input injection

`dart/example_aaos` shows two ways to inject remote pointers: into your own UI (convert the capture-relative `[0,1]` to view coordinates and correct for any offset such as a captured status bar), or device-wide with an `AccessibilityService.dispatchGesture` (screen-absolute coordinates, 1:1 with the capture; drives other apps too; re-check availability on resume). On AAOS, Settings does not list third-party accessibility services, and an emulator reboot resets the enabled list. Enable the service over adb by **appending** to the existing list (it holds the car's own `RotaryService` and `CarSafetyAccessibilityService`), then toggle `accessibility_enabled` 0 → 1 so the system binds it. AAOS runs apps as user 10 — grant with `--user 10`. For a dev rig the example declares `WRITE_SECURE_SETTINGS` (grantable over adb on a development device) and enables its own service on start:

```bash
adb shell pm grant --user 10 <your.package> android.permission.WRITE_SECURE_SETTINGS
```

### Links

The npm and NuGet packages carry these files; paths are from the package root — npm `node_modules/@studioxid/omni-adapter/`, NuGet `~/.nuget/packages/studioxid.omniadapter/<version>/` (Windows `%USERPROFILE%\.nuget\packages\…`):

- This guide: `llms.txt` (the PyPI and pub.dev packages carry it too)
- First connection, step by step in all six languages: `docs/getting-started.md`
- Feature support per language and minimum server: `docs/COMPATIBILITY.md`
- Claude Code skill for adapter consumers: `skills/using-omni-adapter/` — copy the folder into the project's `.claude/skills/`
- The three common examples: `examples/`
- The language reference: the package's `README.md`, also shown on its registry page (npmjs.com, nuget.org, pypi.org, pub.dev)
